narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven by three key factors, ranked by importance. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest influence and unfortunately pushed the prediction toward failure. Even though your 3.3 GPA is slightly above the average of accepted students (3.23), the model determined that this level of performance still increases the risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Next in importance was your performance in the third year of law school. Here the news is more positive: finishing in the 9th decile (well above the 5.8 average of accepted students) pulled the prediction back toward passing. Your LSAT score of 40, which is also higher than the 37.2 average among accepted applicants, provided another modest push in the favorable direction.

In the end, the negative signal from your undergraduate record outweighed the stronger law-school grades and solid LSAT, tipping the model just over the threshold for rejection.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Consider targeted bar-prep courses that address undergraduate-level gaps, maintain or improve your strong law-school performance, and retake the LSAT if you can realistically raise it further. With these adjustments, your profile could clear the threshold on a future application. (248 words)
